title: Stroke Territory Map
description: Interactive map linking the territories of the anterior, middle, and posterior cerebral arteries on a CT-style brain slice to a body figure. Choosing a blocked artery and hemisphere darkens that territory, highlights the opposite face, arm, leg, or half of vision, and lists the typical deficits (typical patterns only; real strokes vary).
creator: Aaryav Sharma
subject: Neuroscience
Stroke
Neuroanatomy
Cerebral Arteries
Clinical Localization
learningObjectives: Given which cerebral artery (ACA, MCA, or PCA) is blocked and in which hemisphere, predict which side of the body and which functions are typically affected.
Explain why a stroke in one hemisphere affects the opposite side of the body.
Distinguish the leg-predominant weakness of an ACA stroke from the face-and-arm-predominant weakness of an MCA stroke and the visual field loss of a PCA stroke.
prerequisites: Visual fields and the occipital lobe (Chapter 5)
Language areas in the left hemisphere (Chapter 12)
keyQuestions: Why does a left-hemisphere stroke weaken the right side of the body?
Why does an ACA stroke affect the leg more than the arm?
Which artery's blockage typically causes vision loss without limb weakness?
Why is aphasia typical of left MCA strokes, while neglect is typical of right MCA strokes?
misconceptions: A stroke affects the same side of the body as the damaged hemisphere.
All strokes cause the same symptoms.
Every stroke causes arm and leg weakness.
The patterns shown are exact rules rather than typical patterns that vary between patients.
controls: Artery select: None, ACA (anterior), MCA (middle), PCA (posterior)
Predict first checkbox: hides the body highlights until unchecked
Click a territory on the brain slice to select it
source: Deficit patterns follow the Selected Stroke Syndromes table, Merck Manual Professional Version, Overview of Stroke (https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/neurologic-disorders/stroke/overview-of-stroke).
limitations: Territory shapes are simplified wedges on a schematic axial slice, not an anatomical atlas. Real strokes vary in size and location and often involve only part of a territory.
